feedback: Check that the model matches the STORY, not just that the number is right: ask 'show me with the counters what happens to the apples.'
If the child combines both numbers (answers 8 for the apples, i.e. 6+2), have them act the take-away story out step by step with counters before counting, tying it to the removing action.
For the joining story, ask 'did the number get bigger or smaller — why?' to connect the action to the operation.
If the set-up is correct but the count slips, scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
activities.intendedInsight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.
learnerActions: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
activities.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat

feedback: If the child adds the two numbers for the part-unknown (4 + 7 = 11), build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters so the gap becomes visible; use a part-whole or bar layout.
For compare problems, if the child adds the two amounts, line the groups up and point to the extra ones to show the difference is what's being asked.
Ask 'how many altogether, and how many do you already know?' to surface which quantity is missing.
Praise a correct layout even before the count, then support careful counting if needed.
activities.intendedInsight: When the unknown is a part or a difference, you still build the situation — lay out what you know and find what's missing — rather than just combining the two numbers you can see.
learnerActions: Model a put-together problem with a missing part, e.g. 'There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?'
Build the whole (7) and lay out the known part (4) using a part-part-whole frame.
Find the gap — the blue counters needed to fill the whole — and count them to give the answer (3).
Model a simple compare problem, e.g. 'how many more', by lining up two groups side by side (a bar/tape layout) and finding the difference.
For each problem, say whether it is a putting-together story or a comparing story, and explain how your drawing matches the words.
activities.title: Part-whole and compare: beyond result-unknown

feedback: Prompt the child to connect language to representation: 'show me the part where things leave.'
If narration drifts from the model, pause and re-anchor each spoken quantity to a group of objects.

Keep the talk tied to acting on objects: the age-appropriate expectation is work with concrete objects and pictorial representations, so narration is intended to accompany modelling rather than replace it.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the story into your own words and linking each phrase to a quantity in your model builds sense-making, so the words guide the action rather than triggering a reflex operation.
learnerActions: Tell an adult or peer what is happening in the story in your own words.
As you narrate, show each step on the objects or drawing ('first there were six… then two fell…').
Answer prompts such as 'which part do you already know?' and 'what are we trying to find?' while pointing to the model.
activities.title: Narrate and show (talk alongside the model)
